title: Thule Inuit migration from Alaska to Greenland
summary: The Thule, ancestors of present-day Inuit, developed around the Bering Strait and spread east across the Arctic, replacing the Dorset culture in the Canadian Arctic and reaching northwestern Greenland. Archaeologists place the main movement around AD 1200-1250; older estimates of about AD 1000 and a late 11th-century arrival are also cited.

uncertainty.note: Years are calendar years AD. Start 1000: the traditional date from Mathiassen (1927) for the Thule development and spread (University of Alaska Museum). The "initial migration from Alaska to Arctic Canada and Greenland" is dated around AD 1200 and the earliest migrants around AD 1200-1250 (Friesen and Norman 2016; midpoint 1225). Parks Canada places the arrival in the eastern Arctic around the end of the 11th century. The waypoint at Smith Sound uses the same general date because the source does not date its sites separately.

importance.justification: The last major prehistoric migration into the Americas, whose descendants are the Inuit of Alaska, Canada and Greenland.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the Smith Sound date is the generic migration date, not a site date; the three points are regions, not dated sites; timing is genuinely debated (AD 1000, late 11th century, 1200-1250, plus a 2022 paper argued in search results that some eastern dates pre-date 1200, not opened). Add Birnirk or Cape Parry site dates and Greenland site dates in the full record.

beats.caption: The Thule whaling and sea-mammal hunting way of life develops around the Bering Strait.
Pioneers move east by umiak through Amundsen Gulf and across the Canadian Arctic in a rapid migration.
Thule settle northwestern Greenland and replace the Dorset culture across the Canadian Arctic; modern Inuit descend from them.
